items.prose: The interviewer: "Write out the numbers 1 to 100. Make me a market on how many 7s you write." Say a fair value and a range. Then work it out.
items.question: How many times does the digit 7 appear?

widget.accept: 20: ten in the units place and ten in the seventies.
widget.label: Count of the digit 7

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the units place and the tens place separately.

byKey.seventy-seven: You counted 77 once. It holds two 7s, one in each place.
byKey.units-only: You counted only the units place: 7, 17, ..., 97. The seventies add ten more in the tens place.

explain.text: The units place shows 7 in 7, 17, ..., 97: ten times. The tens place shows 7 in 70 to 79: ten more, and 77 counts in both. Total 20, which a fair value of about 20 with a range of 15 to 25 would have held.

items.prose: Over a week of mock rounds you gave 50 ranges, each stated at 90%. Thirty-eight held the truth.
items.question: What do you conclude?

options.text: Overconfident: about 45 hits were expected, so widen the ranges.

options.why: You judged the gap by eye. A calibrated forecaster scores 38 or fewer only about 0.3% of the time.

options.text: Underconfident: the ranges are too wide.
options.why: Too wide would give more hits than 45, not fewer.

options.text: Nothing yet: 50 ranges are too few to tell.
options.why: Fifty is plenty for a gap this size. Ten ranges would be too few.

explain.text: Calibrated 90% ranges would hit about $0.9 \times 50 = 45$ times. Scoring 38 or fewer has a chance of about 0.0032 for a calibrated forecaster. The ranges are too narrow, so widen them.

items.prose: A new game: two dice are rolled, and the contract pays the gap between them, the larger minus the smaller. A gap of $d \ge 1$ happens in $2(6 - d)$ of the 36 rolls.
items.question: What is the fair value? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each gap $d$ by $2(6-d)/36$.

byKey.means: You subtracted the fair values, 3.5 − 3.5. The gap is never negative, so its fair value is above 0.
byKey.one-way: You counted each gap one way round. (1, 3) and (3, 1) both give a gap of 2.

explain.text: Gaps 1 to 5 occur in 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2 rolls. So the fair value is $(10 + 16 + 18 + 16 + 10)/36 = 70/36 = 35/18 \approx 1.94$. A simulation of 200,000 rolls with `random.Random(1)` gives 1.945.

items.prose: Three dice. The contract pays the largest face. The largest is at most $k$ with chance $(k/6)^3$.
items.question: What is the fair value? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $E[M] = \sum_{k=1}^{6} P(M \ge k)$.

byKey.two-dice: That is the larger of two dice. A third die pushes the largest higher.
byKey.mode: You priced the most likely value, 6. It happens in only 91 of 216 rolls.

items.prose: A contract pays £10 times (the sum of two dice minus 7). It can pay −£50 up to +£50.
items.question: What is the sd of its payout, in pounds? Give two decimal places.

widget.accept: £24.15: ten times the sd of two dice, 2.4152.
widget.label: sd in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtracting 7 leaves the spread alone; multiplying by 10 scales it by 10.

byKey.shift: You forgot the factor of 10. Scaling a payout by 10 scales its sd by 10.
byKey.variance: That is ten times the variance. The sd scales by 10, the variance by 100.
byKey.root10: You scaled by $\sqrt{10}$. The sd scales by the factor itself.

explain.text: Subtracting 7 moves the fair value to 0 and leaves the spread unchanged. Multiplying by 10 multiplies the sd by 10: $10 \times 2.4152 = 24.15$. A quote of ±£24 holds about two thirds of outcomes.

items.prose: Three dice. The interviewer allows a width of 5, and you quote 8 to 13. The totals 8 to 13 occur in 21, 25, 27, 27, 25 and 21 of the 216 rolls.
items.question: What share of rolls does your quote hold? Give four decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the six counts and divide by 216.

byKey.totals-equal: You treated the 16 totals as equally likely: 6/16. Count rolls, not totals.

explain.text: The counts add to 146, so the share is $146/216 = 73/108 \approx 0.68$. The sd of three dice is 2.96, and whole-number totals make 8 to 13 act like $10.5 \pm 3$. That is about one sd each side, and a normal holds 0.68 there.

items.prose: A share trades at £50 with a daily sd of 2%, or £1. You quote fair value ±£1. A takeover rumour doubles the sd.
items.question: What half-width keeps the same share of moves inside your quote, in pounds?

widget.accept: £2: twice the sd, so twice the half-width.
widget.label: Half-width in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the half-width at one sd.

byKey.same: You kept the old width. The rumour doubles the moves, so you would be picked off.
byKey.variance: You scaled by the variance, four times. Width scales with the sd.

explain.text: The half-width was one sd, £1. The rumour doubles the sd to £2. So the quote widens to £48 at £52.

items.prose: The interviewer: how many £1 coins, laid edge to edge, make a mile? A mile is about 1,600 m, and a £1 coin is about 2.3 cm across.
items.question: Which answer would you give?

options.why: You divided metres by centimetres. Convert the mile to 160,000 cm first.
You kept every figure from rough inputs. Give one or two significant figures.
You added two powers of ten. 160,000 ÷ 2.3 is about 70,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put both lengths in centimetres, then divide.

explain.text: A mile is about 160,000 cm, and $160{,}000 / 2.3 \approx 70{,}000$. With the exact figures, 1,609.344 m and 2.25 cm, it is 71,526. One significant figure is the honest answer: about $7 \times 10^4$.

items.prose: Your Fermi estimate has four factors. Two are good to a factor of 2. One is good to 1.5, and one to 3.
items.question: In the worst case, the total is good to a factor of what?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Error factors multiply.

byKey.added: You added the factors. In logs they add, so the factors themselves multiply.
byKey.worst: You kept only the worst factor. The others compound with it.

explain.text: In logs the doubts add: $\ln 2 + \ln 2 + \ln 1.5 + \ln 3 = \ln 18$. So the worst case is a factor of 18 either way. Pin down the factor of 3 first: it is the biggest doubt.

items.prose: A contract pays £1 per square, of any size, on a chessboard. Before you count, the interviewer buys 2 from you at 220. Then they sell you 1 at 200. You count: 204.
items.question: What is your total P&L at the true value, in pounds?

widget.accept: £36: +32 on the sale and +4 on the purchase.
widget.label: P&L in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark each trade at 204 and add.

byKey.net-only: You marked only the one contract you are still short. Both trades count against 204.
byKey.sign: You treated the purchase as a loss. Buying at 200 something worth 204 gains £4.

explain.text: Selling 2 at 220 against 204 earns $2 \times 16 = 32$. Buying 1 at 200 against 204 earns 4 more. The ledger ends short 1 with +£36.
